newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt features in minor metals, others quiet.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt features in minor metals, others quiet.

text.p: Cobalt was the main feature of trading in the industrial minor metals market this week, with a majority among traders polled by Reuters forecasting higher prices by the end of 1996.
But several European traders remained unconvinced that cobalt had the potential to spike higher.
"Consumers are still holding off in anticipation of lower numbers," one said.
Upside sentiment was strongly reinforced by a lack of prompt material and concerns over the situation in Zaire.
Traders also kept an eye on Zambia where Frederick Chiluba was sworn in for a second term as president after he rejected opposition charges that he rigged a landslide election victory.
He said security forces would be alert for any political unrest.
Several traders reported good demand from Japan and Hong Kong.
"The market is tight in the Far East...we have had to air freight material in," one said.
"There is scant if any offers for prompt material," another added.
One trader suggested Russian material could reach $25 a pound by the end of 1996 against the backdrop of demand from the aerospace, battery and chemical industries.
Traders leaning towards the bearish end of the market said consumer demand was slow but did agree that stocks available to the market remain low.
"The higher numbers been mentioned in the market are unrealistic," one trader said basing his view on an apparent lack of end-user covering.
Elsewhere conditions remained slow following this week's Metal Bulletin ferro-alloys conference held in Istanbul.
Many major European traders attended.
Antimony steadied amid the lack of Chinese offers and a belief that the recent slide in prices had bottomed out.
Although the use of cadium in Japan has slowed, China and India have been quick to soak up any availble material for nickel/cadium batteries.
Brisk demand for bismuth was seen in the U.S.
"Both cadium and bismuth have the potential to head higher near-term" one trader said. "There is reasonable demand growing."
Molybdenum, also seeing a lack of Chinese offers, snapped higher. Traders said nearby material was scarce, while any available material was already committed to long term contracts.
